_meta.directives: Fiche recentrée sur le nom (2026-10-03). Chaque piste d'origine est attribuée à qui la porte et citée à la page dans les notes de sa source ; aucune n'est retenue comme la bonne. Sakiliba et Danba sont des noms de femmes, non des graphies de Sissoko : ne pas les verser dans les graphies. Ne pas étendre sans source dédiée.

oralTraditions.claim: In the account of the division of lands at Kouroukan Fougan, the Sunjata epic says of the people of Fakoli, the Koroma, that others call them Doumbouya or Sissoko; this people receives the monopoly of the forge and of ironworking. The name thus appears there as another name of Fakoli's lineage, without the account saying where it comes from.
oralTraditions.carrier: Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté, griot de Djeliba Koro, près de Siguiri
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane, qui l'a traduit en français

oralTraditions.claim: Sissoko and Doumbia are said to come from one and the same family, the two names replacing each other according to region. The same survey places Sissoko among the bula, a group of families that it says came mostly from the Siendougou, in the Sibi region, near Bamako.
oralTraditions.collector: Molinie, officier de la marine française, en 1959
oralTraditions.context: Origins recorded from oral tradition for a dictionary written for the use of Europeans posted in French West Africa, cited at second hand in a thesis of 2017; the informant is not named

writtenChronicles.claim: In his N'ko work on the names and jamu of the Manden, Souleymane Kanté gives Doumbia as the jamu of the men of the lineage and Danba as the jamu of the women. Under the entry Kourouma, he lists among the equivalents a form that the translation transcribes as Sìisɔ́ɔ̀, and that the thesis translating it links to Sissoko.

historicalSyntheses.claim: A historical synthesis makes the Sissoko, the Doumbia and the Koroma the descendants of Fakoli Koroma, whom the oral traditions of the Manden record as one of Sunjata's generals. It does not say where it takes this link from, nor how or when the three names would have separated.

linguisticReconstructions.claim: No dictionary or linguist's work consulted gives a meaning for the word: the dictionary of Mandinka clan names defines it only as a clan name, and the thesis that brings together the sources on these names reports no explanation of its origin.

The dictionary of the jamuw has an entry Sisɔkɔ, with the variant Sisoko. It gives three clan names there as equivalents: Dantɛ, Dunbiya (Doumbia) and Kuruma (Kouroma), and the entry Bàgayɔgɔ (Bagayoko) in turn gives Sisoko as an equivalent. The dictionary does not say what this equivalence covers, nor which form is the oldest.

The women of the lineage bear a different clan name from the men. Under the entry Sisɔkɔ, the dictionary gives Danba for the women of griot families (jèli) and Sakiliba for those of free families (hɔ́rɔn). It also glosses Sakiliba as the feminine name corresponding to Dunbuya (Doumbia), and gives Sakiliba as an equivalent of Danba. Sakiliba is therefore not another spelling of Sissoko: it is the name borne by Sissoko women of free families. A contributor to a Soninke community forum, for their part, writes the names Sakiliba, Boula, Sora and Damba after Sissoko, marking Damba as feminine.

casteOrSocialFunction.value: The dictionary of the jamuw gives three statuses under the entry: jèli (griot), nùmu (blacksmith) and tontigi, a term that it glosses under the entry of another name as that of cultivators. Area mentions follow the last two: among the Maninka after nùmu, among the Bamana after tontigi. The same name therefore covers different social conditions according to area and lineage, and none of these statuses is attributed to all the families that bear it.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Appendix of clan names of the Bamadaba, the electronic Bambara-French dictionary of the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA), pointed out by Vydrin in Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. Complete file consulted. The entry Sisɔkɔ (variant Sisoko) carries three statuses (jèli, nùmu among the Maninka, tontigi among the Bamana), three equivalences (Dantɛ, Dunbiya, Kuruma), two feminine forms (Danba among the griots, Sakiliba among free families), a prohibition, nkaana, which the file does not translate, and three markers of a people, which Bogacheva's thesis reads as Maninka, Bambara and Kagoro. The entry Sakiliba glosses it as the feminine name corresponding to Dunbuya; the entry Danba gives Sakiliba as an equivalent; the entry Bàgayɔgɔ gives Sisoko as an equivalent. The entry Sisɔkɔ gives no meaning for the name and no joking partner.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, IV : L'Afrique du XIIe au XVIe siècle — chapitre 6, Le Mali et la deuxième expansion manden
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. D. T. Niane, 1985; chapter by D. T. Niane. Printed page 157: Fakoli Koroma (or Kuruma) among the generals of Sunjata whose names the oral traditions have retained, and note 42, according to which his descendants are the sisoko, dumbuya and koroma clans. The chapter gives no meaning for the name.

sources.title: Les noms de clan du Manden (jamu) dans les sources africaines, occidentales et arabes
sources.notes: Bogacheva, E. A., undergraduate thesis, Saint Petersburg State University, 2017, in Russian; supervised by A. Davydov, read by V. Vydrin. Entry Sisɔkɔ, pp. 124-125: Maninka, Bambara and Kagoro peoples, the prohibition nkaana, and, after Souleymane Kanté's N'ko work, the jamu Doumbia for men and Danba for women (p. 125). Entry Danba, pp. 29-30: equivalent of Sakiliba (p. 29), and feminine jamu of the Sissoko after Kanté (p. 30). Entry Dunbiya, p. 38: Sissoko and Doumbia from one and the same family, and Sissoko among the bula who came mostly from the Siendougou, after the dictionary of Molinie, an officer of the French navy, 1959, who says he recorded these origins from oral tradition. Entry Kuruma, p. 97: the form Sìisɔ́ɔ̀ among the equivalents, after Kanté. Entry Sakiliba, p. 114. Kanté's original N'ko text was not read; only its Russian translation was. An undergraduate thesis is not a peer-reviewed publication: it is cited for the testimonies that it relays.

sources.title: Soundjata ou l'épopée mandingue
sources.notes: Niane, Djibril Tamsir, Présence Africaine, 1960. Transcription of the account of the griot Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté of Djeliba Koro (Siguiri); it is a written record of an oral tradition. Page read in the digitised copy on archive.org (SoundjataOuLepopeeMandingue), close to the printed edition without being identical to it: the people of Fakoli, the Koroma, whom others call Doumbouya or Sissoko, and their monopoly of the forge (p. 141).

sources.title: Nom de famille ?
sources.notes: Discussion thread of the forum of the community portal Soninkara.com, held from 21 June to 5 July 2006 by contributors under pseudonyms, consulted directly. One of them writes, on 5 July 2006, after Sissoko, the names Sakiliba, Boula, Sora and Damba, marking Damba as feminine, without giving its meaning. The thread does not say where the name comes from; several participants point out that the same name can be found in different groups and statuses according to region and family history.

sources.title: Relevé de couverture anthroponymique EthniAfrica
sources.notes: This name appears in our list of names to cover: it was selected as a name to document, but no dedicated source has yet been consulted. The fiche therefore exists to flag the name, not for what it asserts about it. Forthcoming checks will draw on electoral registers, national statistical institutes and onomastic studies of the country concerned.

gaps.reason: The meaning of the name is not established in the sources consulted. General-audience content puts some forward, but they are incompatible with one another (an animal, a people or a region, a knowledge) and none cites a linguistic study: we retain none of them.

The only account found that names its teller does not say where the name comes from; the griot whose interviews a 2017 thesis relays does not speak of it. We have not found a published account of the origin of the name among the griot families who bear the form Cissokho in Senegambia.

The dictionary of the jamuw links the name to the Maninka, the Bamana and the Kagoro, but not to the Soninke, and the Soninke grouping called Wago does not count this name among its own. The link to the Soninke rests only on a community discussion thread: it is given as presumed. We do not yet have a page devoted to the Kagoro.

Only Mali is supported. The name is also found in other countries of the region, notably in the form Cissokho, but we have not found a quantified or documented source specific to this name for those countries.

The dictionary of the jamuw gives no joking partner (senankuya) for this name. A 2017 thesis places Sissoko among those of the Berete without saying where it takes this link from, and the dictionary does not repeat it: we attest no alliance.

We name no bearer. Fakoli, to whose lineage the epic and a synthesis attach the name, is called Fakoli Koroma there, not Sissoko; no source consulted links a deceased person to this name in its own words.
The spellings Sissako, Cissokho and Sissokho exist, but no source consulted says that they designate the same lineage: they are not merged here.
